jsonld.description: Molokhia is the leaf that divides the world's eaters: Jew's mallow, corchorus — a green that cooks to a dark, faintly viscous soup-sauce the Nile valley has loved since the pharaohs' kitchens, served over rice or bread with a rabbit or chicken. The leaf's slipperiness is its identity and its gift — the texture that the Egyptian kitchen celebrates and the uninitiated must meet on its own terms — and the technique is its own: the leaf minced fine (frozen, pre-minced molokhia is the working truth abroad), simmered briefly in a rich broth, and finished with the takliya — a fried garlic-coriander flash poured sizzling over the pot. The rabbit is the traditional animal; the chicken is the common week's own.

skeleton:
Molokhia with Rabbit

Egyptian · Hard · Serves 4

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Molokhia is the leaf that divides the world's eaters: Jew's mallow, corchorus — a green that cooks to a dark, faintly viscous soup-sauce the Nile valley has loved since the pharaohs' kitchens, served over rice or bread with a rabbit or chicken. The leaf's slipperiness is its identity and its gift — the texture that the Egyptian kitchen celebrates and the uninitiated must meet on its own terms — and the technique is its own: the leaf minced fine (frozen, pre-minced molokhia is the working truth abroad), simmered briefly in a rich broth, and finished with the takliya — a fried garlic-coriander flash poured sizzling over the pot. The rabbit is the traditional animal; the chicken is the common week's own.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

Ingredients

- **Thaw and dry the frozen molokhia fully (or mince the fresh to near-paste).** The frozen leaf is the diaspora's staple and entirely honest — thawed, it holds the mince's fineness that the fresh demands by hand. The leaf must be dry before it meets the broth: wet molokhia waters the sauce's viscous body. - **The bridge:** molokhia itself is unbridgeable — the leaf's texture is the dish — and it is carried frozen in every Egyptian, Levantine, and many Asian groceries (look for "molokhia" or "mulukhiyah," minced, frozen). The rabbit bridges to chicken truly; the coriander seed is the takliya's non-negotiable partner.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The broth: deep, strained, one notch past salted before the leaf joins.
  • The leaf: jade green, viscous-silky, the 10-minute ceiling held.
  • The takliya: 90 seconds' gold, poured as a cap, never stirred.

Molokhia with Rabbit

Prep: 40 minutes · Cook: 1 hour 10 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 55 minutes · Serves 4

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 1 rabbit (about 1.2 kg), cut to 8 pieces — or 1 kg bone-in chicken thighs
  • 400 g fresh molokhia leaves, stripped and minced very fine — or 400 g frozen minced molokhia (the working truth, about 400 g thawed)
  • 2 onions (about 300 g): one quartered for the broth, one minced for the serve
  • 6 cloves garlic (about 25 g), divided: 4 pounded for the takliya with 1 tbsp ground coriander seed (about 6 g), 2 sliced
  • 2 tsp ground coriander, divided; 1 tsp cardamom pods or ½ tsp ground (the broth's perfume); 1 bay leaf; salt
  • 3 tbsp neutral or #95 smen (about 40 g); 1.8 litres water (about 1.8 kg)
  • To serve: rice (300 g cooked), the #116 cumin salt, lemon wedges, and the #2 koshari's sharp pickles or vinegar-soaked onion

Instructions

  1. **The broth (45 minutes).** The water brought to the barest simmer — roughly 95 °C, the surface's shiver — the rabbit pieces browned lightly in the fat; add the quartered onion, the whole spices, the bay, and 2 of the garlic cloves; the water — bring to a bare simmer, cover, and cook 40–45 minutes until the rabbit is tender to the bone and the broth runs deep. Lift the rabbit to a warm bowl, strain or skim the broth, and salt it one notch past comfort — the leaf will calm it. Checkpoint — the broth: a rich, faintly perfumed gold, deep enough that a spoon's coat holds — the molokhia's sauce-to-be. The rabbit at the bone's twist, held warm. The strained broth returned to the pot at a bare simmer.
  2. **The leaf's brief swim (10 minutes — the clock that matters).** Whisk the minced molokhia into the simmering broth — it disperses to the pot's dark green — and simmer just 8–10 minutes, stirring twice: the leaf cooks fast, and over-cooking both darkens the green past its jade and breaks the viscous body into stringiness. The rabbit returned to warm through in the last 2 minutes. Checkpoint — the molokhia's body: the broth turned a deep jade green and faintly viscous — the spoon's coat running slow, the texture silky-thick, never gluey or stringy. The color's jade is the clock's proof: dull olive means over. Taste — the leaf's green, faintly bitter-mineral depth over the broth's richness, the salt now balanced.
  3. **The takliya — the sizzling crown (2 minutes).** In a small pan, fry the pounded garlic and the ground coriander in the remaining fat (or a fresh spoon of butter) until the garlic's fragrance rises and the edges just gold — 90 seconds — and pour the whole sizzling spoonful over the molokhia's surface. Do not stir: the takliya sits as a perfumed cap, each ladle from the pot carrying its share. Checkpoint — eating test, over rice, the rabbit beside: the molokhia's jade silk — viscous, green, mineral-deep, the broth's richness carrying — the takliya's fried garlic-coriander arriving in bursts, the lemon's cut and the cumin salt at the table, the rabbit's tender savory against the leaf's character. It should taste like the Nile's own argument — a texture the world must meet, and a flavor that repays the meeting.

Finish & Plate

The pot to the table — the takliya's cap visible on the jade — the rabbit fanned beside, the rice's mound ready, and the lemon, cumin salt, and sharp pickles at every hand. The ladle serves the pot's layers together.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Molokhia stringy, olive-darkOver-simmeredThe 10-minute ceiling; pull at jade
Body thin, wateryWet leaf or weak brothDry the thawed leaf; the broth's depth first
Takliya bitterGarlic browned past goldThe 90-second fry, watched

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- The broth keeps 3 days refrigerated (the leaf always swims fresh in the day's broth — the frozen mince's own economy: a bowl at a time); the takliya fries in its minute. The #2 koshari and the #18 lablabi are this record's fellow Nile pots on this site. - Variations: the chicken week's version, the shrimp-coastal Levantine cousin, the rabbit festival's own. The rabbit bridges; the leaf never does — and that is the recipe's one law.
